text: >> Doctor Armstrong, thank you for your time. Appreciate it.
Let's start off by asking what your message is to
community members who are upset about this plan.
>> Yeah. Well, I want them to know that there has been
a lot of thought and planning and consideration that went
into developing the scenarios that they're seeing, and that
we understand that communities are special places for
schools, and we have to continue to do what's best
for Portland Public Schools as an entire school district.
>> Do you think that you have the votes for this to get it
through the school board?
What I'm hearing is that, I mean, the outcry
from the public already before they've even seen
the details is significant.
And you may not have the votes with the school board. Yeah.
Are you confident do you have the horses for this?
>> Well, I'm confident that they're ready to
engage in conversation about sustainability.
You know this all started with board direction
and the resolution asking me to look at right
sizing to sustain our.
Our schools and our our financials. Really.
And then from there, they developed guiding principles
that served as guardrails.
And then we took that to get into the details.
And so what community is seeing is our best thinking.
We expect feedback, push back comments, questions.
We welcome it.
And it will all lead to a final recommendation to
the board on November 17th.
>> You mentioned budget concerns. Is this.
Is this mainly about money?
>> It's not. And I think that's a common misconception
that closing schools doesn't serve or does not address all
of your financial woes. Right.
The budget concerns that we have moving forward
is a structural deficit.
So we need to address that.
Now, there are some savings that are realized through closing
schools like those fixed costs, the deferred maintenance,
the ways in which we care for our buildings, but generally
staff follow our students.
And with staff being about 90% of our budget, it's tough to
say that it solely is a, um, a strategy for saving money.
>> Yeah. I think your chief operations officer said a few
months ago that it really wasn't about money, but maybe that was
just a mischaracterization.
It's not just about money.
>> It's not just about money.
It would be the correct statement.
I mean, we want to find savings in everything that
we do, and rightsizing gives us an opportunity to
save some of those funds.
But it won't address our $65 million deficit alone.
>> The savings is that is that coming from long
term capital expenses?
I mean, if you close schools, then you don't have
to necessarily retrofit them or renovate them.
And if that's the case, you know what happens to the bond
money, the $4 billion in bonds that we passed since 2012.
Does that money, where does that money go?
>> Yeah, that's an excellent question.
So we definitely hope to see savings through um,
things or savings realized with fixed costs. Right.
So that is the maintenance and upkeep of the building.
Some of the repair work things like that.
And when we think about bond funds, we've had significant
investments in remodels, renovations and even seismic.
And if there are funds that are currently allocated to
a building that's up for close, then we'll reallocate
those funds rightsizing it.
>> It seems to sound like a euphemism for perhaps layoffs,
significant disruptions to families in the community.
I mean, explain to me what rightsizing really means.
>> Yeah. So I would say simply, it's about getting to the right
size in the portfolio of schools that we have so that
we can sustain our schools and then resource better.
Like that's the hope.
The right sizing plan, as you see, doesn't show that we'll
have all schools over 360.
We'll still have schools that are low enrolled.
What it does do is it provides us an opportunity
to sustain in greater areas across our city so that we
can begin to resource better.
>> A school board member asked recently how many
layoffs this will create.
Do you have that number yet?
>> I don't have that number, and a lot of people are
wanting us to put that math with the the closure plan.
And what I tell them is that the state school fund is set
by the governor, and she will release that, and then it
will go into the legislative session, and we'll be waiting
to see what that final vote is.
And so as we get early information, we can start to
make some predictions to begin to think about our annual
budget planning process.
But our numbers aren't final until that
legislative session closes.
>> Is this going to increase class sizes?
>> Well, I hope not. The goal is to resource better, and we
know that when we're able to resource better, we're able
to lower that class size.
I will say that a lot of people out there want me to
state a number and say, we're committed to this number,
and that's hard to do when we don't yet know what our state
school fund will be.
And so the best that I can say is that we want to lean
towards what our average is, which is around 25 to
26 in our primary grades.
And in some cases in our city, we have class sizes
that are well into the 30s, and we have some class sizes
that are under ten, and we need to get to a balance.
>> We are about six weeks away from this school
board vote in December.
If you're a parent or a student and your school is on this list,
what kind of data would they need to provide to you in order
to get themselves off the list?
>> Yeah. Well, first, I will say that we do want to spend
the month of October engaged in public discussion.
We'll be out to school sites, impacted sites.
We want to continue to have listening sessions
both virtual and in person and with our school board.
So there'll be many opportunities to give input.
I mean, I think if I were a parent showing up,
I actually send to kiddos to Portland Public Schools.
So I think what I would want to hear is about the way
in which they cared for the community, the way in
which they cared for staff.
I want to know about the facility
and the complexity of that.
I definitely would want to know about walkability
and safe routes to school, and the capture rate and other
opportunities, not just the, you know, what are we doing
the right size now and over the next few years, but how
are we going to aggressively pursue students that live
within the Portland City?
That capture rate is what I'm talking about.
How are we going to aggressively pursue those
students and showcase what, um, what our school or our
district has to offer?
And as a parent, I would be really interested in
knowing that.
>> These listening sessions, I mean, do you foresee
the possibility that that the parent input or
the student input might lead to changes in the list?
Or is it strictly performative?
>> Yeah, that's a great question.
And we actually expect it to lead to changes.
So what you see now are two scenarios that we're
presenting to the community.
And then as we engage in this pretty ambitious community
engagement calendar and we get into the process of
feedback, um, I suspect that there'll be some changes
and some adjustments.
It will all help inform that final recommendation
that I submit to the board on November 17th.
And then the board will have several weeks to sit
with that and then vote.
Um, the way that I explain it to community is that
the board will really have three choices before them.
Vote for the superintendent's recommendation.
Vote for the recommendation with some changes or defer
the decision.
And those are the choices that I foresee being
before the board.
>> Yeah. I was going to ask, is it, uh, you know.
When we see these things unfold, these big decisions, a lot of
times the most likely outcome is just pausing the decision.
You know, kicking the can down the road. Could that happen?
>> It could happen.
The board could decide to defer to a later time.
Um, what will have to do is continue to be creative about
the ways in which we support schools while realizing that
we have, at this point a $65 million reduction.
But again, that can change.
We don't have the state school fund balance yet.
We haven't calculated in recommendation from
the governor as of yet.
And so that number could go down.
We don't anticipate it going up because we're basing it
off of what the state school fund is now.
>> There is significant criticism out there
regarding the district's management of funds, the $65
million deficit, saying the school could do better.
The amount spent per student, the test scores.
Can the district do better?
And what's your plan?
>> Well, we're a learning organization and we always
center ourselves as learner, and I think we
absolutely can do better.
We definitely want to continue to improve in the way we respond
and support individuals.
And I appreciate you highlighting the criticism.
There is criticism out there wondering if there was
a mismanagement of funds.
When we think of the $65 million reduction, this is a reduction
that's built over time.
I entered as superintendent in 2024, and for that
fiscal year, it was already communicated that we would
need to reduce 40 million.
The second year then was 56.
So that's almost $100 million in reduction.
And in this final year, the 65 million that we're predicting
will end our structural deficit.
So it's actually quite the opposite.
We're looking to stabilize the district for the first
time in a very long time.
And then as a follow up, the other thing that I'll say
to that is there's also lots of criticism about other ways in
which we spent money speaking about our bond program.
And a lot of people confuse the bond program with funds
that could be spent to reduce our deficit.
And bond funds are for buildings.
Our voters voted on, you know, standing up three
renovated high schools.
We've broken ground on two of the three.
The third one will be November 13th.
And we're excited about that work that's moving forward.
>> So there's no co-mingling of those funds into your
your general budget, right.
>> Those are very specific, um, uses attached to it.
>> Okay. What's the single most important factor when you,
when you create this list of recommendations for closures?
What's the single most important factor for closing a school?
>> Yeah. I would say the single most important
factor for us is the way in which we send our students,
the way we work to keep our school communities together.
Um, more often than not, meaning being clear about where
that body of students move together with their peers, um,
is extremely important.
I would say that well-rounded experience in making sure that
our students are able to access art and music and physical
education where there's multiple grade levels in the classroom,
where there's class sizes that are manageable and that we're
supporting our learners, our students every day coming in
to school are coming in with more complex needs, and we want
to be able to address it with resources and ways that allow
them to thrive.
>> You've talked about the need for well-resourced schools.
Are there schools right now that are you consider
not well resourced?
>> Oh yeah. Absolutely.
Well, any time that we've had to spend like over the last
eight years pulling funds from our larger schools to subsidize
our smaller schools, that means that there are some schools
that are going without.
And that's the reality that we're in.
You know, I have set out to do superintendent site engagements
where I visit schools and then spend time either in the morning
or the afternoon sitting with that community educators
and often students, and they have really good questions.
And the way I explained it to one student, it's like,
you know, you're going to a fair and you have a set,
um, budget and you have six people with you.
The amount that you spend is going to be vastly
different if you have three people to spend on.
So I like to talk about what it means to have a set of
funds and then being able to figure out how to stretch that
dollar as far as you can.
And they seem to pick up on that.
>> A lot of staff members have been asked to push back their
cost of living increases until January. I believe.
At the same time, you did receive a significant
raise, and there's been some pushback regarding that.
Do you want to set the record straight as far as, uh, if you
feel that that was justified?
>> Yeah, I appreciate that question.
And I think there's some misconception in that. Right.
My employment agreement was negotiated upon my
hire back in 2024 and was under current market rate.
And so while it made the news several months ago,
the rate and the raise was determined back in 2024.
What I did ask for, though, is that Mykola be capped.
So in 2024 it was 3% no matter what.
And so what I asked the board for was to make sure that
it's never greater than what our teachers receive.
So if our teachers then settle at 2%, then Mykola would be 2%.
And so moving forward, that was an adjustment down.
And that's what showed up in the employment agreement.
>> You stepped into this in 2024.
Obviously, you have to play the hand that you're dealt.
I is the district top heavy when it comes to,
you know, management positions in this building
relative to the teachers who are on the front lines
and the educators and the, you know, the administrators.
>> Yeah, we have been.
So the data has shown that Portland, at the administrative
level, the percentage was a little higher than comparison
districts.
And we've been addressing that over the last couple of years.
We've reduced Central Office last year by 14%.
And this year, when we get into the annual budget
process, I will lead out with my recommended
reductions that start off with my executive team.
>> Demographics obviously play a big role in this.
You know, declining class sizes.
Is that the only factor when it comes to declining
class sizes, or is it?
Have you considered the possibility that there
are families out there who are less than satisfied
with your product.
You know, given the test scores.
You know, and they're choosing to go to private
school or they're choosing to go to online school.
Have you factored that in?
>> We have, and I actually appreciate you asking
that question, because it gives me an opportunity to
clarify a couple of things.
Like Portland as a city isn't the only city that's on decline.
Every major urban city is seeing a decline in enrollment.
And in fact, Oregon State has lost 40,000 or I should
say, not lost, because the kids could be out there.
But we're 40,000 fewer than we were in 2019.
That's a lot of students over a course of 6 or 7 years.
And the other thing that I will say is that
birth rates are down.
Like that's the number one reason why we're
seeing this decline across the United States.
And that will continue to be true until people start
having more babies again.
And when they do, we'll still have an adequate
number of schools to be able to house those students.
Um, but again, I, I appreciate the question.
And I also know that there are options and choices
that that families seek.
Another data point that I'll give is that I will say about
a decade ago, our capture rate was in the mid 80s.
I don't think there's ever been a time when Portland has
been above 90%, at least in the last couple of decades.
Right now we're about in the mid 70s.
And so we know there's an opportunity to capture
families, recapture families that live within
our our boundary.
And we will be working really hard to really tell the story
of our schools and make sure they know that our classrooms
are exceptional places to learn and to grow.
And that's our current effort now and into the future.
>> So we are out of time.
Any last words?
Anything that I didn't address that you want to convey to
the people of Portland?
>> Well, I just want our families to know that we
recognize that this is a hard time, and we have
things that are coming out that's overwhelming,
shocking, and concerning.
And we are going to commit to continuing to be early
and often with our information and communication.
And I will invite families to access our website at
www.net/rightsizing, where they can access dashboards and maps
and data and frequently asked questions.
That's the best source to get information.
So basically, stay out of the comments on social media.
Don't be drawn to the sensationalized titles.
We have all the information and the data attached to back up
the claims that we're making.
>> Doctor Armstrong, I do appreciate your
time. Thank you so much.
>> Yeah. Thank you so much.
